To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
banks' CTA adoption choice under the IFRS 19 implementation is associated with bank specific fundamental factors, opportunistic factors related the application of IRRS 9 and bank risk taking.

(1) banks that adopted the transitional arrangements under IFRS9 (CTA) reduced their systematic risk exposure, (2) the reduction in systematic risk exposure is more significant for banks operating in countries where the power of the national banking authority is higher.

(1) banks' adoption of the CTA policy is associated with neutral and opportunistic factors; (2) the adoption of the C TA is negatively associated with bank systematic risk, and such a relationship varies depending on the power of the bank regulatory authority.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential opportunistic behavior of banks in the adoption of the CTA policy.
how banks respond to the new IFRS 16 accounting standard and the associated CTA policy.
the impact of the adoption of IFRS9 on the banking system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adoption of CTA policy by banks is associated with a lower exposure to systematic risk.
the CTA adoption is a rational response of the banking sector to the new accounting standard IFRS 16.
the CTA policy is a successful policy to mitigate the adverse effect of the IFRS 6 on the banking system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CTA policy can be an effective tool to reduce bank risk exposure, and the banking authority can use it as an effective policy to control bank risk taking behavior.
banks that adopt the CTA are less risky and more likely to be subject to a more powerful banking authority.
the CTA policy is a useful tool for the banking authority to reduce bank systemic risk and to mitigate the negative impact of the IFRS 8 adoption.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the CTA adoption is associated with bank risk taking, which is in line with the argument of the Basel Committee that the CTA is a transitional tool for banks to adjust to the new IFRS 16 requirements.
banks' CTA adoption choice can be explained by both neutral and opportunistic motivations.
the CTA is a policy that is not fully effective in mitigating banks' risk-taking behavior, especially for banks operating in jurisdictions with weak banking authority.
